A slide's 'builds' gives, per part, the share of the narration at which it appears.

title.en: FundsXML explained: one language for fund data

subtitle.en: What it is for, who uses it, and how to start

description.en: A ten-minute overview of FundsXML, the open XML standard for exchanging fund data in Europe: the problem it solves, what it covers, how asset managers, administrators, distributors, insurers and data vendors use it, how data quality is checked, and how a project gets started. With a look at a real FundsXML file in FreeXmlToolkit.

say.en: FundsXML in ten minutes. You learn what the standard is for, who uses it, what it covers, and how to get started. No knowledge of XML is needed.

en.title: Fund data travels a long way

say.en: Behind every investment fund, data travels a long way. The asset manager, the fund administrator and the custodian bank produce it. Distributors and fund platforms, data vendors, insurance companies and regulators need it: prices and net asset values, portfolios, costs, and a growing number of regulatory templates. Every one of these parties exchanges data with many others.

items.head: Every pair of partners agrees on its own files
items.text: Field names, codes and layouts differ from one interface to the next.

items.head: A new partner means a new interface
items.text: Mapping, testing and maintenance start again from scratch.

items.head: Every new rule is built many times
items.text: When regulation changes, each interface has to follow on its own.

items.head: Errors surface late
items.text: Often only at the receiver, when the data is already in use.

say.en: Without a common format, every pair of partners agrees on its own files, with their own field names and codes. A new partner means a new interface, with mapping and testing from scratch. When regulation changes, every one of these interfaces has to be changed on its own. And errors surface late, often only at the receiver, when the data is already in use.

items.head: Valuation
items.text: The administrator calculates NAV and positions.

items.head: Asset manager
items.text: Checks the figures and adds fund data.

items.head: Distribution
items.text: Prices, costs and ESG data go to platforms.

items.head: Insurers
items.text: Receive the portfolio look-through.

items.head: Vendors & regulators
items.text: Get master data, prices and reports.

say.en: Take a single fund at month-end. The fund administrator calculates the net asset value and the positions. The asset manager checks the figures and adds its own fund data. Prices, costs and ESG data then go to fund platforms and distributors. Insurance companies that hold the fund need the full portfolio look-through. And data vendors and regulators receive master data, prices and reports. One fund, one date, and the same data travels to five places or more.

FundsXML is the answer: one common language for fund data. Instead of many bilateral formats, every party writes and reads the same format. A sender produces a file once, and every receiver understands it, in the same way.

items.head: Open and free
items.text: The schema and its documentation are published openly and free of charge.

items.head: Made by the fund industry
items.text: Developed since the early 2000s by asset managers, banks and service providers.

items.head: Built on XML
items.text: A mature, widespread technology: every system can read it, every file can be checked automatically.

items.head: Works alongside other standards
items.text: It complements ISO 20022, FIX and openfunds, with a focus on fund data.

say.en: FundsXML is open and free. The schema and its documentation are published, and anyone can use them. It is made by the fund industry itself, and has been developed since the early two thousands by asset managers, banks and service providers. It is built on XML, a mature technology that every system can read, and every file can be checked automatically. And it does not compete with other standards: it works alongside ISO 20022, FIX and openfunds, with a clear focus on fund data.

items.head: Fund master data
items.text: Funds, sub-funds and share classes, identifiers, fees.

items.head: Prices and NAV
items.text: Net asset values, prices and fund volumes in any currency.

items.head: Portfolios
items.text: Positions of all asset classes, linked to the securities' master data.

items.head: Transactions
items.text: Trades, subscriptions, redemptions and distributions.

items.head: Regulatory data
items.text: The European templates for costs, ESG and look-through.

items.head: Country modules
items.text: National reporting, for example for Austria and Germany.

items.head: Documents
items.text: Links to prospectuses, reports and other fund documents.

items.head: Signatures
items.text: Digitally signed files: the receiver sees who sent them.

say.en: What does FundsXML cover? First, the fund's master data: funds, sub-funds and share classes, with their identifiers and fees. Then prices and net asset values. Portfolios, with positions of every asset class. And transactions. FundsXML also carries the European regulatory templates: EMT for costs and target markets, EPT for PRIIPs, EET for ESG data, and TPT, the look-through for insurers. Country modules add national reporting. Fund documents can be linked, and a file can be digitally signed.

items.head: ISIN
items.text: Identifies securities and share classes.

items.head: LEI
items.text: Identifies companies: the fund, the manager, the issuer.

items.head: ISO codes
items.text: For currencies and countries.

items.head: Fixed lists
items.text: For asset types, cost types, fund types and many more.

say.en: FundsXML relies on common codes instead of free text. An ISIN identifies a security or a share class. An LEI identifies a company: the fund, the asset manager or an issuer. Currencies and countries use their ISO codes. And fixed lists describe asset types, cost types or fund types. So every receiver interprets a value in exactly the same way, without guessing.

en.headline: One file, many receivers.
en.sub: The same delivery serves the distributor, the insurer and the data vendor. Each one takes the part it needs.

say.en: This is the key idea: one file, many receivers. The same delivery can serve the distributor, the insurer and the data vendor. Each one takes the part it needs.

Let us look at a real file. This is one of the public FundsXML example files, opened in FreeXmlToolkit, a free XML editor. It describes one fund on one reporting date: the fund itself, its share classes and its portfolio.

Folded, the structure is easy to see. Control data says who sent the file, and for which date. Funds holds the fund itself, with its prices and portfolio. Asset master data describes every security once, and the positions refer to it.
Every value has a clear name. Here is the fund's total net asset value, in euro. A machine can process it, and a person can still read it.
A file is also a source for analysis. The Query Console of FreeXmlToolkit comes with ready-made FundsXML queries. This one lists the ten largest positions of the fund.
Shown as a table: every position with its name, its market value and its weight in the fund. The same query works on any FundsXML file, from any fund house.

en.title: Who uses FundsXML, and for what

items.head: Distribution
items.text: Asset managers send costs, target markets and ESG data to distributors and platforms.

items.head: Insurance
items.text: Insurers receive the full portfolio look-through for their capital requirements.

items.head: Fund administration
items.text: Administrators and custodians deliver holdings, prices and NAVs.

items.head: Data vendors
items.text: Vendors and platforms collect master data and prices from many fund houses.

items.head: Investor information
items.text: Data for key information documents and factsheets.

items.head: Regulatory reporting
items.text: Fund data for supervisors and central banks, with the country modules.

say.en: Who uses FundsXML, and for what? Asset managers send costs, target markets and ESG data to distributors and platforms, for MiFID and SFDR. Insurance companies receive the full look-through of a fund's portfolio, which they need for Solvency II. Fund administrators and custodian banks deliver holdings, prices and net asset values. Data vendors and platforms collect master data and prices from many fund houses, in one format. The data also feeds key information documents and factsheets. And it serves regulatory reporting to supervisors and central banks.

items.head: Fund portfolio
items.text: All positions of the fund, with their master data.

items.head: TPT data
items.text: The Tripartite Template, carried in FundsXML.

items.head: Insurer's systems
items.text: Load the data of every fund the same way.

items.head: Solvency II
items.text: Capital requirements, based on the real holdings.

say.en: Here is one example in more detail. An insurance company holds fund units, and Solvency II asks it to look through to the real holdings. So the asset manager delivers the fund's full portfolio, with the master data of every position. The Tripartite Template, TPT for short, travels inside FundsXML. The insurer loads the data of all its funds in the same way, and calculates its capital requirements on the real holdings.

items.head: Senders
items.text: Produce one format for all their partners, instead of one per partner.

items.head: Receivers
items.text: Load data from every fund house the same way.

items.head: Everyone
items.text: Automatic checks before the data moves on.

items.head: Lower cost of change
items.text: A new regulatory requirement is built into the standard once.

say.en: What does each party gain? Senders produce one format for all their partners, instead of one per partner. Receivers load data from every fund house the same way. Everyone can check a file automatically, before the data moves on. And when regulation changes, the new requirement is built into the standard once, and not into every single interface.

items.head: Readable
items.text: A well-formed XML file that any system can open.

items.head: Valid
items.text: It fits the FundsXML schema: the right fields, data types and codes.

items.head: Plausible
items.text: Business rules hold: weights add up, identifiers check out.

say.en: Quality is built in, on three levels. First, the file must be readable: well-formed XML that any system can open. Second, it must be valid: it fits the FundsXML schema, with the right fields, data types and codes. Third, it must be plausible: business rules hold, for example portfolio weights add up, and identifiers like ISIN codes have correct check digits.
Tools do these checks for you. In FreeXmlToolkit, one click creates a data-quality report for the open file.
The report lists every check, and whether it passed. A receiver can run the same checks, and both sides talk about the same findings.

items.head: Scope
items.text: Which data, for which partner?

items.head: Mapping
items.text: Your fields to FundsXML elements.

items.head: Examples
items.text: Start from the public sample files.

items.head: Validate
items.text: Schema and business rules.

items.head: Pilot
items.text: One partner, real data.

items.head: Go live
items.text: Automate and monitor.

say.en: How does a FundsXML project run? Start with the scope: which data, for which partner. Then map your own fields to the FundsXML elements; this is usually the biggest step. Start from the public example files, not from an empty page. Validate early, against the schema and the business rules. Run a pilot with one partner and real data. Then go live, automate the deliveries, and monitor them.

en.title: Free to use, from day one

items.head: The schema
items.text: github.com/fundsxml/schema

items.head: Example files
items.text: github.com/fundsxml/examples

items.head: Documentation
items.text: fundsxml.org

items.head: Tools
items.text: FreeXmlToolkit and other XML tools

say.en: Everything you need to start is free. The schema and the example files are on GitHub. The documentation is on fundsxml dot org. And free tools, such as FreeXmlToolkit, open, check and explore FundsXML files.

items.head: Start small
items.text: One data area, one partner, then extend.

items.head: Agree on the details
items.text: Which optional fields, which codes, which delivery times.

items.head: Check on both sides
items.text: The sender validates before sending, the receiver before loading.

items.head: Keep test files
items.text: Good and bad examples that every change is tested against.

say.en: A few tips from practice. Start small: one data area and one partner, then extend. Agree on the details: which optional fields you fill, which codes you use, and when the data arrives. Check on both sides: the sender validates before sending, and the receiver before loading. And keep a set of test files, good ones and bad ones, so that every change can be tested against them.

items.head: Every file names its version
items.text: In its control data, next to the sender and the date.

items.head: New releases mostly add
items.text: New elements are usually optional, so existing files stay valid.

items.head: Partners agree on a version
items.text: And move to a newer one when they are ready.

items.head: Every change is documented
items.text: In the changelog that comes with the schema.

say.en: How do new versions fit in? Every file names the version it was written for, in its control data. New releases mostly add elements, and these are usually optional, so existing files stay valid. Partners agree on the version they exchange, and move on when they are ready. And every change is documented in the changelog that comes with the schema.

items.head: Regular releases
items.text: New versions follow new regulation and market needs.

items.head: Practitioners decide
items.text: Changes are discussed and agreed by people who use the standard.

items.head: Your voice counts
items.text: Report issues and propose changes on GitHub.

say.en: FundsXML is a living standard. New versions follow new regulation and the needs of the market. Changes are discussed and agreed by the people who use the standard every day: asset managers, administrators, banks and service providers. And your voice counts: you can report issues and propose changes on GitHub, and every proposal is discussed in the open.
That was FundsXML in ten minutes. To go deeper, continue with the series FundsXML basics: it shows the standard step by step, in a real file. Thanks for watching.
